messages.subject: dsm bug in smoothing parameter estimation
messages.subject_clean: dsm bug in smoothing parameter estimation
messages.body_plain:
Hi listfolk,

This is a warning for those using the DSM engine within Distance and the
dsm R package.

The latest mgcv update (1.8-23, release onto CRAN 2018-01-15) has
changed the behaviour of the gamma= option. Previously this was ignored
by the default fitting method in dsm, REML. Now the gamma argument is
passed when gamma is specified with REML or ML.

The previous behaviour of dsm was to set gamma=1.4 for models fitted
with GCV (as suggested in Kim & Gu, 2004). This was ignored when REML or
ML were used. The new behaviour is that "smoothing parameters are chosen
as if the sample size was n/gamma instead of n" (see
https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/mgcv/ChangeLog), giving rather
different estimates.

A new version of dsm is now on github and will appear on CRAN soon. It
will use gamma=1 for all methods. This will be incorporated into the
next version of Distance for Windows. In the meantime, setting gamma=1
explicitly in your models will get back to the "old" behaviour (sample
size =n) when method="REML" or method="ML". Those using method="GCV.Cp"
should set gamma=1.4 manually.

We continue to recommend folks use REML or ML for their models, as this
has strong theoretical basis for optimal smoothing at finite sample
sizes. But please ensure that gamma is set to 1 for REML/ML, unless you
have some specific reason to change it.

You can check previously run models by inspecting the model$call$gamma
and model$call$method elements, if your model is called "model". (A
gamma value of NULL means the default of 1 was used.)

Apologies this took a while for me to notice.

best,
--dave

--

References:

Kim, Y. and Gu, C. (2004), Smoothing spline Gaussian regression: more
scalable computation via efficient approximation. Journal of the Royal
Statistical Society: Series B (Statistical Methodology), 66: 337-356.
doi:10.1046/j.1369-7412.2003.05316.x

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] Help beach transects
messages.body_plain:
Hello Eric,

Thank you again for the advice and answers! I think this group is a very important space for those using this method, and your willingness to respond and help is to be praised.

We decided to change the approach of beach transects to prevent these large areas of overlap in coverage areas between legs of the zigzag. So, we tried a design of 20 transects of 10 meters in a straight line, also equally spaced by 10 meters, which would give an area of: 400m length x width of the beach. In this way we would not have this overlap problem.

We measured the width of the beach at the beginning and divided by 2, and there was the beginning of the transect.

The results of the analyzes surprised me, I think it resulted in good detection probability curves, and low coefficients of variation. The only drawback is with larger size classes (class L and XL) that do not have a probability of detection = 1 in the transect line. Most of these objects were furthest from the transect line. Do you think this will be a problem if we take this method?

size L: between 10 cm and 1m
size XL: > 1m

I did several analyzes, one analysis without any truncation, another with a truncation of 5% of the largest distances, analyzes by size classes (with and without truncation), and analyzes with truncation at 20 meters distance.

In wider beaches, we were thinking of doing 2 lines of 10 transects of 10m side by side, and a continuous line of 20 transects of 10m on the narrowest beaches.

I would really appreciate if you could see the analyzes of this test we did, and say if there is something that is not working, or is there any parameter that should be better? Any suggestions. I'll send the project by email, ok?

Once more, thank you for the help,

Sara

Hi Sara,

Just a couple of points:

1. I would not have the transects parallel to the coast line, but perpendicular to the coast line, to avoid density gradients (I wonder if this is somehow related to the second problem). As you have it you are oversampling some areas which are not random with respect to litter distribution.
2. It seems weird that g(0) is not 1 for the largest classes. Since g(0) is the probability of detecting an object on the line, I would expect it to be lower for the smaller classes?

Any way, maybe this is a discussion to have off the list.

cheers

Tiago

messages.subject: RE: [distance-sampling] Help beach transects
messages.body_plain:
Yes, as Tiago says, lines should not be parallel to the shoreline.  Your design creates two major problems.  First, your design is a single line with gaps, not replicate lines, so variance estimates will be invalidated.  (For wider beaches, you would have 2 lines.)  Second, objects will not be uniformly distributed with respect to distance from the line.  You see this with your large objects, which are relatively unlikely to be recorded in the middle of the beach I imagine.  You’re interpreting the distribution of distances from the line as if it reflects probability of detection, but it is more likely that it largely reflects varying density of objects as you move up the beach.

I think you should either have transects along the beach and attempt complete counts (possibly with gaps as per your design, and possibly using more than one observer walking line abreast) or have lines perpendicular to the shore line, and use distance sampling.  If the latter, decide what is a reasonable truncation distance.  If you adopt say 20m, then put the lines a minimum of 40m apart, and for each line, record anything detected within 20m of the line.  Ideally each line will run from the top of the beach to the low water mark.

This may be impractical, but your design will not yield valid analysis, so a different compromise may need to be found.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject_clean: Model selection affects adjusted ungulate counts
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Hoping you can help me answer some questions related to issues that I am having understanding the results of my analyses.

Quick outline of my study design and what I plan to analyze:

I am studying three target ungulate species: bighorn sheep, elk, and mule deer. I have stratified my study area into “open” areas and “forested” areas, as detection of ungulates will most certainly differ in each of these habitats. Thus, I wish to model each of these 6 datasets (3 species x 2 habitats) with a separate detection function then calculate the probability of detection for each dataset. Distances were calculated from observer to group centroid exactly (distances were not binned in the field). I am using CDS as a way to adjust summed ungulate counts within sampling units across my study area. Each sampling unit has a mean distance from unit to survey transect. I will later model each species’ habitat use using adjusted species counts and environmental covariates as predictor variables.

Here is the general approach that I have followed for each dataset (separately):

-Fit a simple preliminary model (half-normal key + cosine adjustment) to explore the non-truncated datasets

-Examined histograms for failure to meet distance sampling assumptions (ie: heaping at 0 distances, movement prior to detection, rounding distances etc.)

-Determined truncation distances based on g(w) = 0.15

-Fit same 6 potential models to 6 datasets

-Examined AIC, chi-sq GOF, and K-S GOF results

-Selected top model then calculate probability of detection and adjusted counts within sampling units

I have attached a spreadsheet (Model_Comparisons).

Questions:

Q1:

>From everything I have scoured within this forum, and from the Buckland et al. (2001) book, I understand that I should select the top model based on AIC, while also ensuring that my data meet GOF tests. For example, in my open bighorn analysis, the top model based on AIC was the uniform key function with a cosine adjustment term (with 3 orders). The GOF chi-sq p-value 0.490 > 0.05 and the GOF K-S p-value 0.79 > 0.05. The QQ plot showed that the model fit the data well, as did the histogram (screenshots attached). This is how I selected the top models for each of my 6 datasets (selected top models are highlighted in attached spreadsheet). When competing top models were within 2 AIC values (and each model adequately met GOF tests and QQ plots & histograms showed good model fit), I rationalized that this meant each model could adequately represent my data and, thus, it didn’t really matter which model I selected. So, I still went with the lowest AIC value to retain consistency in my approach. I also understand that when there are competing top models, I could model average or I could consider the model that is most parsimonious, as AIC tends to select for models with more parameters (or less-parsimonious models). I do not wish to model-average as I would argue that any of my top models should be adequately able to adjust my ungulate counts sufficiently. Does this approach make sense? Am I missing something?

Q2:

When I went to actually calculate the probability of detection for each species x habitat type, I ran into some issues. Take ‘open elk’ for example. I’ve included my R script used to calculate probability of detection, as well as the top model output for ‘open elk’ from Distance 7.1, below. The top model, based on my approach listed in Q1, is the half-normal key function with no adjustment terms. When I calculated the probability of detection based on y distances, the probabilities ranged from 0 to 0.99. The adjusted counts, therefore, ranged from 2.42 x E39 groups per sampling unit to 0 groups per sampling unit. Obviously, something is wrong because there is no way that there are 2.42 E39 elk groups in a small sampling unit. After experiencing this issue, I decided to adjust counts based on the other competing top model from ‘open elk’ to see if I could get better estimates and to cross-reference. This was the uni+cos model (model output and R script below). I’ve also attached a spreadsheet that compares the probabilities of detections and adjusted counts for each competing top model for open elk (the spreadsheet is a subset of my data). Basically, what I have found is that I was not at all correct with assuming that just because both of these models came out as “competing top models” that they could equally represent my data. So, why are my adjusted counts so biologically illogical? Does this mean that I should not be selecting my top models in the manner I described in Q1? Why are the adjusted counts for the half-normal so different from the adjusted counts from the uniform+cosine, when both models are within 0.64 AIC values and meet the model fit standards that I described in Q1? Are the adjusted counts poor because I am extrapolating detection functions determined from right-truncated data (400 m for open elk dataset) to distances > 400 m? Should I remove data > 400 m from my habitat use analysis, since I cannot accurately predict detection of ungulate groups past this distance? This would certainly limit the application of my results as I would have a much smaller effective study area. Are my data not meeting some assumptions that I somehow missed in my data examination? How should I proceed to accurately adjust my counts for detectability while ensuring they are biologically relevant?

Thanks in advance,

Meghan Beale

University of Alberta

Department of Biological Sciences

Line transect data that have a spike close to the line are notoriously difficult to model. I'm not sure what the scale was on the x-axis but I'm guessing km, so

walking a short distance apart, side by side (it's important to be sure

messages.subject_clean: "perception bias" VS "visibility bias": Does distance sampling take it into account already?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

My question is related to the concept of "visibility bias", which lead us to the use of the probability of detection to account for not seen animals."Visibility bias" can be distinguished in "perception bias" and "availability bias". I had the feeling that in literature the definition and differences of the two types of biases is not vey clear. My understanding (based on Marsh ans Sinclair 1989) is that:

-perception bias, represents the animals that are potentially visible to the observers but are not seen (because we cannot see very far due to human limits for instance).
-availability bias, represents the animals that are not available to observers because they are concealed by other animals, vegetation, or turbid water.

My opinion is that "availability bias", as it is defined in that paper, it is implicitly included in the "perception bias". Also, when we use line-transect distance sampling method we use the distributoon of the observations to identify the best model of probability of detection. One of the characteristics of this distribution is the ESW, which can be different I think depending on the density of the vegetation (for instance). Therefore, do we really need to correct for visibility bias? Is it not already took in to account when we build the "probability function of detection"?

Best,

GS

messages.body_plain:
Hi Gabriele,

I agree that the two concepts do blend into each other in the limit, but they are nonetheless useful to describe and talk about distance sampling.

Conventional distance sampling (CDS) corrects for perception bias, i.e. for all the reasons that might make you miss an animal that is available to be detected but is not. It does so by assuming that the major contributor to model the detection function is distance from the transect.

If animals are not available to be detected, i.e. if availability bias is present, then CDS won't help you., There is nothing in the detected distances that tells you whether 3% or 97% of say desert tortoises are in burrows.

Under some settings, MRDS (using double platform methods) can be used to estimate availability bias, provided all animals have a non-zero chance of being detected. If some animals have probability 0 of being detected, remaining unavailable for detection for the entirety of the survey duration, then you need independent information (besides distance sampling data) about this availability bias to estimate the total population size, since at best you can estimate from the data the available (to detection) population.

Hope this helps

Tiago

messages.body_plain:
If concealment by vegetation is considered to be availability bias, then this CAN be accounted for by modelling the detection function.  Using CDS, it simply assumes that animals can’t be concealed by vegetation if they’re on the line, but can be at greater distances from the line.  There is no need to distinguish between this and perception bias.  However, if you have considerable heterogeneity, so that for example an animal might be readily detectable at 50m at some points along the line, but hidden at 2m at other points, then we’re unlikely to model that detection function satisfactorily.

Steve Buckland

messages.body_plain:
Oscar

Seems your model has quite a few adjustment terms.  One "ad hoc" approach might be to force the fit of a model with sufficiently few adjustment terms such that a GOF test has degrees of freedom to produce a test result.  If that GOF test (with few adjustments) shows adequate fit, then it seems probable that a model with more adjustments would fit even better.

Alternatively, you may need to resort to visual assessment of fit, rather than quantitative.  That is the challenge presented by binned data--there is less information available to assess fit.
